dryRun.title: countChars("banana")
dryRun.note: One pass, six steps. Every step does the same thing: read the current count (or 0), add 1, store it back. After the last step the map answers any "how many" question in O(1).

think.q:
const count = {}
for (const ch of 'aabc') count[ch] = (count[ch] || 0) + 1
console.log(count.a, count.c, String(count.z))
why: a appears twice, c once. z was never counted, so the key does not exist and the lookup gives undefined, not 0.
Trap: forgetting that a missing key is undefined. Use (count[z] || 0) when you need a number.

think.q:
const c = {}
for (const ch of 'aa') c[ch]++
console.log(String(c.a))
why: The first time, c.a is undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN. Once a count is NaN, it stays NaN forever.
Fix: start from zero with c[ch] = (c[ch] || 0) + 1, or use Map with m.get(k) ?? 0.

think.q:
const m = new Map()
for (const n of [1, 1, 2]) m.set(n, (m.get(n) || 0) + 1)
console.log(m.get(1), m.size)
why: The value 1 is counted twice and 2 once, so m.get(1) is 2. The map has two distinct keys, so m.size is 2, not 3.
Trap: reading size as the number of items in the input. It is the number of distinct keys.

think.q: You must check whether two lowercase words (only letters a to z) are anagrams. Which counting structure is best?
opts: A nested loop that removes matched letters one by one
A Map that you sort by key before comparing
An array of 26 numbers, one slot per letter
A Set of the letters of each word
why: With a fixed alphabet, counts[ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97]++ is fast and uses O(1) extra space (26 slots).
A set forgets how many times a letter appears, so "aab" and "abb" would look equal. Trap: using a set when counts matter.

think.q: You count the letters of "listen", then subtract one for every letter of "silent". When are the two words anagrams?
opts: When the map has no keys left
When the last subtraction gives a negative number
When both words have the same first letter
why: Same letters with the same counts cancel each other exactly. Any count that is not 0 means one word has an extra or a missing letter.
Trap: checking only the keys. A map can keep a key whose value is 0, so look at the values.

try.task: Write isAnagram(a, b). Return true if b uses exactly the same letters as a, the same number of times (any order). Both strings may contain any characters.
try.hint: Count the letters of a, then walk through b and subtract. If a count goes below zero (or the lengths differ), return false.

checks.verify: assert(isAnagram('listen', 'silent') === true, 'listen / silent should be true')
assert(isAnagram('rat', 'car') === false, 'rat / car should be false')

checks.t: counts matter, not only which letters appear
checks.verify: assert(isAnagram('aab', 'abb') === false, 'aab / abb should be false')
assert(isAnagram('ab', 'abc') === false, 'ab / abc should be false')

takeaway.key: Frequency counting turns "how many of each?" into one O(n) pass and O(k) space, where k is the number of distinct values. Read the count (or 0), add 1, store it back.
mistakes: Doing count[x]++ on a key that does not exist yet, which gives NaN.
Using a Set when the number of occurrences matters.
Comparing two maps with ===. Compare them key by key, or subtract one from the other.

dryRun.title: middle of 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
dryRun.note: Fast covers two nodes for every one node of slow. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered exactly half the list, so slow is the middle. No length counting, no second pass.

think.q:
const list = (a) => a.reduceRight((next, val) => ({ val, next }), null)
let slow = list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), fast = slow
while (fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next }
console.log(slow.val)
why: Slow moves two times (1 to 2 to 3) while fast moves 1 to 3 to 5. Fast has no next, so the loop stops with slow on 3.
Trap: counting from the middle of the values instead of the nodes you actually visit.

think.q:
const list = (a) => a.reduceRight((next, val) => ({ val, next }), null)
let slow = list([1, 2, 3, 4]), fast = slow
while (fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next }
console.log(slow.val)
why: With an even length there are two middles (2 and 3). This loop condition (fast && fast.next) ends on the second one, which is 3.
If you need the first middle, stop earlier with fast.next && fast.next.next.

think.q:
const a = { val: 1, next: null }, b = { val: 2, next: null }, c = { val: 3, next: null }
a.next = b; b.next = c; c.next = b   // 3 points back to 2
let slow = a, fast = a, steps = 0
while (fast && fast.next) {
  slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; steps++
  if (slow === fast) break
}
console.log(slow === fast, steps)
why: Step 1: slow is on 2, fast is on 3. Step 2: slow is on 3, and fast goes 3 to 2 to 3, so both stand on 3. They meet, so there is a cycle, after 2 steps.
A cycle traps fast inside the loop, and fast gains one node on slow every step, so they must meet.

think.q: In a list without a cycle, how does the fast and slow loop end?
opts: Fast reaches null (or the last node) and the loop stops
Slow and fast meet at the middle
why: Fast moves faster, so it always reaches the end first. The check fast && fast.next stops the loop there, and the answer is "no cycle".
Trap: checking only fast.next. If fast is already null, reading fast.next crashes.

think.q: You must detect a cycle in a linked list and you are not allowed to use extra memory that grows with the list. What do you use?
why: Fast and slow pointers use two variables, so the extra space is O(1). A set of nodes would take O(n).
Both run in O(n) time. The difference is memory.

try.task: Write middleValue(head). The list is made of nodes like { val, next }. Return the val of the middle node. For an even length, return the second of the two middle nodes.
try.hint: Move slow by one node and fast by two. Loop while fast and fast.next both exist.

checks.t: even length gives the second middle

takeaway.key: Two pointers at different speeds share one pass: when fast finishes, slow is at the middle; if there is a cycle, fast catches slow. Time O(n), extra space O(1).
mistakes: Checking fast.next without first checking fast, which crashes on even-length lists.
Forgetting that an even-length list has two middles, and returning the wrong one.
Using a Set of nodes when the problem asks for O(1) extra space.

dryRun.title: 2nd largest of [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4] (k = 2)
dryRun.note: The heap never holds more than k = 2 numbers: the two biggest seen so far. The smallest of them sits on top, so peek() is the 2nd largest: 5.

think.q: console.log([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4].sort((a, b) => b - a)[1])
why: Sorted from big to small: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Index 1 is the 2nd largest, which is 5.
This works but costs O(n log n). A heap of size k does the job in O(n log k).

think.q: console.log([10, 9, 1].sort().join(','))
why: Without a compare function, sort turns the numbers into strings and sorts them as text. As text, "10" comes before "9".
Always write sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers.

think.q: You need the k largest numbers of a very long list. Which heap do you keep, and how big?
opts: A min-heap that never holds more than k numbers
A max-heap that never holds more than k numbers
A min-heap with all n numbers
A max-heap with all n numbers
why: The top of a min-heap is the smallest of the kept numbers, so it is the first one to throw away when a bigger number arrives. What stays are the k largest.
Trap: using a max-heap of size k keeps the k smallest instead.

think.q: A list has n numbers and you keep a heap of size k. What is the time cost of the whole scan?
why: Each of the n numbers does one push and at most one pop on a heap of size k, and each costs O(log k). So the total is O(n log k).
When k is much smaller than n, this beats sorting (O(n log n)). Space is O(k).

think.q: Numbers keep arriving one by one, and after each one you must report the top 3 so far. What is the best idea?
opts: Sort the whole list after every new number
Keep a min-heap of size 3 and update it
Scan the whole list three times
why: A heap of size 3 updates in O(log 3), which is constant. Sorting after each number would cost O(n log n) every time.
This "keep only the best k" idea is exactly what a top-k heap is for.

try.task: Write kthLargest(nums, k) with the MinHeap given in the starter. Push every number. When the heap grows bigger than k, pop the smallest. At the end, return the top of the heap.

checks.t: k equal to the length gives the smallest

takeaway.key: To get the k largest, keep a min-heap of size k: push each number, pop the smallest when the heap is bigger than k. Time O(n log k), space O(k).
mistakes: Using a max-heap of size k, which keeps the k smallest.
Calling sort() on numbers without a compare function, so 10 sorts before 9.
Letting the heap grow to n numbers, which loses the O(n log k) advantage.

dryRun.title: directed graph 0 → 1 → 2 → 0
rows: mark 0 as "visiting", look at its neighbour 1
0 is still "visiting": we came back to a node on our own path
dryRun.note: A node marked visiting is on the path we are walking right now. Meeting it again means the path loops back: a cycle. A node marked done is safe to meet again.

think.q:
// buggy: only remembers "visited"
const g = { 0: [1, 2], 1: [3], 2: [3], 3: [] }
const seen = new Set()
const dfs = (n) => {
  if (seen.has(n)) return true
  seen.add(n)
  return g[n].some(dfs)
}
console.log(dfs(0))
why: It prints true, which is wrong: this graph has no cycle. Node 3 is reached from 1 and again from 2. The second time it is already in seen, so the code says "cycle" even though 0, 1, 2, 3 never loop.
In a directed graph, meeting a visited node is not enough. It must be on the current path.

think.q: In a directed graph, which three states does each node need during DFS?
opts: not visited, visiting (on the current path), done
why: "Visiting" means the node is on the path from the start to here. "Done" means all of its neighbours were fully explored. Meeting a visiting node is a cycle; meeting a done node is fine.
The diamond graph (0 to 1 and 2, both to 3) is why two states are not enough.

think.q: In an undirected graph, edge A - B means A is a neighbour of B and B is a neighbour of A. When DFS goes from A to B and sees A again, why is this not a cycle?
opts: Because B has no other neighbours
Because A is B's parent, and it is the same edge, not a new one
why: In an undirected graph, the edge you just used shows up again from the other side. A real cycle is when you meet a visited node that is not your parent.
So undirected detection passes the parent along: dfs(next, node). Union-Find is another way.

think.q: A graph has V nodes and E edges. What is the time cost of DFS cycle detection?
why: Each node is entered once and each edge is looked at once (twice in an undirected graph, which is still O(E)). So the total is O(V + E).
Space is O(V) for the states and the recursion path.

think.q: A course list says "take 1 before 0" and "take 0 before 1". You must tell whether all courses can be finished. What is this problem?
opts: Cycle detection in a directed graph
why: Courses are nodes, "before" rules are directed edges. You can finish everything only if there is no cycle. Here 0 needs 1 and 1 needs 0, so it is impossible.
This is the idea behind the problem Course Schedule, and it leads straight to topological sort.

try.task: Write hasCycle(n, edges) for a directed graph with nodes 0..n-1. Each edge is [from, to]. Return true if the graph has a cycle.
try.hint: Keep a state per node: 0 = not visited, 1 = visiting, 2 = done. If DFS meets a node in state 1, return true. Set the state to 2 when you leave a node.

checks.t: a diamond is not a cycle
the cycle is not reachable from node 0

takeaway.key: Directed graph: DFS with three states (not visited, visiting, done). Meeting a visiting node means a cycle. Undirected graph: meeting a visited node that is not your parent means a cycle. Time O(V + E).
mistakes: Using only a visited set on a directed graph, which reports a false cycle on a diamond.
Forgetting to start DFS from every node, so a cycle in a separate part of the graph is missed.
In an undirected graph, treating the edge back to the parent as a cycle.
